opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it comes down to the fact that reinforcement learning is only as good as the signal you're optimizing against. In domains where RL has had its biggest wins, like games such as Go or Atari, or more recently math and coding with language models, you have a very clean reward. You either won the game or you didn't. The proof checks or it doesn't. The unit tests pass or they fail. That clarity lets you scale RL really aggressively, because the agent can try millions of things and you can trust that the signal is telling it something true about the task.

Robotics doesn't have that. Take something as simple as folding a shirt or loading a dishwasher. What does success actually mean? Is the shirt folded "well enough"? Did you put the plate in at a slightly wrong angle that'll cause a problem later? Writing that down as a reward function by hand is extremely hard, and when people try, the policy usually finds some way to exploit it. It satisfies the letter of the reward without doing what you wanted. That's reward hacking, and in the physical world it's especially painful because every rollout is expensive. You can't just run a billion episodes overnight like you can in simulation.

So you end up with two compounding problems. First, the reward is hard to specify, so the signal is noisy or gameable. Second, data collection is slow and costly, so you can't brute-force your way past a noisy signal with sheer volume. In games, even a sparse reward is fine because you can simulate endlessly. In robotics you get neither a dense, trustworthy reward nor cheap samples.

That's why a lot of robotics has leaned on imitation learning: you sidestep the reward problem by just copying demonstrations. But imitation caps you at roughly the level of the demonstrator, and it doesn't really teach the system to recover from its own mistakes. The thing that made RL so powerful elsewhere was getting superhuman behavior by optimizing beyond the data, and you can't do that without a reward you trust.

So to me, the interesting frontier is learned reward models and general-purpose verifiers: using large vision-language models, for example, to judge whether a task was done correctly, the same way we've started using models as judges in language. If you can get a reward signal that's general, robust, and hard to hack, a lot of the RL machinery we already have starts to just work. But until then, I think the reward is the bottleneck, more than the algorithms themselves.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so if you think about what reinforcement learning actually is, it's a system that learns from experience, from trial and error. And the thing that makes trial and error work is that you have some signal telling you whether what you just did was good or bad. That's the reward. In a game like Go or chess or Atari, that signal is basically free. The environment gives it to you. You won, you lost, you got points. It's clean, it's dense enough, and it's perfectly aligned with what you actually care about.

Robotics is the opposite situation. Say you want a robot to fold a shirt or load a dishwasher. What's the reward? You could try to hand-write one, something like distance of the plate to the rack, but you very quickly find the policy exploits whatever proxy you wrote. It'll jam the plate in sideways, or knock everything else out, because the number you wrote down isn't the thing you actually meant. And the thing you actually meant, "the dishwasher is loaded well," is a fuzzy, perceptual, human judgment. It's not something you can write as a function of joint angles.

So you end up in this situation where the learning algorithm is actually pretty good. We know how to optimize a reward if you give us one. The bottleneck is that nobody can give us one. And the two workarounds people use both have problems. One is to collect demonstrations and do imitation learning, which gets you a decent starting point but caps you at the level of the demonstrator and doesn't let the system improve on its own. The other is to put a human in the loop giving feedback, which is the right idea but it's extremely expensive if you need it on every single episode.

I think the interesting version of this, and it's what we've seen play out in language models, is that you want a learned reward model. Something that has enough general understanding of the world that you can show it a video of the robot and it says, yeah, that counts as a folded shirt, or no, that's not it. Once you have that, RL in robotics stops being a search for a reward and becomes a compute problem, which is a much better problem to have. That's really why I frame it as the fundamental bottleneck. The algorithms scale, the hardware is getting there, but if you can't tell the robot what good looks like, none of the rest matters.

astra-6.text:
The core issue is that reinforcement learning needs a signal that tells it whether it’s doing something useful. In a game, that signal is built in: you get a score, you win or lose. You can run the game millions of times, and it tells you how you did.

In robotics, you have to supply that judgment yourself. Say you want a robot to clean a kitchen. What exactly counts as success, and how does the robot detect it? You could write a reward for moving objects off the counter, but putting everything on the floor would satisfy that reward without accomplishing what you wanted.

And even if you can reliably recognize a clean kitchen, that signal might only arrive after a long sequence of actions. The robot still has to discover which actions led to success. So you have both a specification problem—what do we actually want?—and a learning problem—how do we provide enough feedback to learn it efficiently?

That’s why rewards are such a bottleneck. Having a robot collect more experience doesn’t automatically help if you can’t evaluate that experience. You need a scalable way to tell the robot whether it’s making progress across all the different tasks you want it to do.

sol-6.1.text:
The core issue is that reinforcement learning tells you how to optimize a reward, but it doesn’t tell you where that reward comes from. And in robotics, specifying the reward can be almost as hard as specifying the task itself.

Say you want a robot to clean a kitchen. What does success look like? You can’t just reward it for moving objects, because it might move them to the wrong place. You need a signal that captures whether the kitchen is actually cleaner, whether things are put away correctly, whether anything was broken. And you need that signal across all the situations the robot might encounter.

For a narrow task in a simulator, you can often hand-engineer that signal because you have access to the underlying state. In the real world, you mostly have observations, like camera images. Now you need to infer whether the robot succeeded from those observations. Sparse success signals can also make exploration very difficult: the robot may try a huge number of things without ever getting useful feedback.

So even if you have a very capable policy and a good reinforcement learning algorithm, you still need a scalable way to tell the robot what’s good. That’s why I see reward as such a fundamental bottleneck.
